title: Can You Predict a Ruling from Oral Argument?
hook: Courtroom folk wisdom says the side that gets grilled hardest is the side that loses. Someone finally checked the numbers — and the rule works, but barely better than a coin flip.
key_points: The folk rule: justices aim more questions and words at the side they doubt, so question counts should forecast votes.
Feldman tested it on 495 individual justice votes across 56 cases; the word-imbalance rule called about 64% of them correctly.
Accuracy varied hugely by justice — above 75% for some, close to random for others, so no single rule reads the whole bench.
For picking case winners the signal was weaker still, and did not beat simply always betting on the petitioner (~68%).
Counterintuitively, argument was most revealing in 5-4 splits (~82%) and least in unanimous rulings — the close cases leak the most.
Heavy questioning can signal a case's importance rather than a justice's skepticism, which is where the rule misfires.
content_html: Anyone who has watched a Supreme Court argument has heard the folk rule: count the questions, and whichever lawyer takes the harder beating is the one about to lose. The intuition is reasonable — justices press on the arguments they doubt. Writing at SCOTUSblog, Adam Feldman put the rule to an empirical test.
extra_html:
Feldman scored 495 individual justice votes across 56 cases using a word-imbalance measure — which side of the argument absorbed more of a justice's words — and found it predicted roughly 64% of votes. Better than chance, but well short of a crystal ball, and the average hides a lot: the rule tracked some justices above 75% of the time while performing close to random for others. Predicting the case winner proved harder than predicting individual votes, and notably the models did not beat the simplest possible baseline — always bet on the petitioner, who wins about 68% of the time. That gap is the real lesson for anyone reading predictions: a model only earns attention when it outperforms the obvious guess.

The most surprising result runs against intuition. Argument was most informative in 5-4 decisions, where vote accuracy reached about 82%, and least informative in unanimous ones. Feldman notes cases where the questioning pointed the wrong way entirely, a reminder that a hot bench can signal that a case is hard or consequential rather than that a particular advocate is losing.

related.title: Nine Justices, Nine Styles
related.hook: One scholar coded 5,095 questions from a full Supreme Court term and found each justice interrogates lawyers in a signature way — a fingerprint of how they think about the law.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

related.title: Why No Cameras in the Supreme Court?
related.hook: You can read every Supreme Court ruling, but you can't watch the arguments on video. The long fight over courtroom cameras is really a fight over judicial transparency.

prereqs.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
prereqs.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

flashcards.prompt: What is the courtroom folk rule about oral argument and how a justice will vote?
flashcards.back_html: That justices direct more questions and words at the side they are skeptical of — so whichever advocate gets grilled harder is the one likely to lose.

flashcards.prompt: In Feldman's analysis, when did oral argument reveal the most about how justices would vote?

choices.text: In unanimous cases, where the bench agrees
Equally across all cases, regardless of how divided

flashcards.explanation_html: Vote accuracy reached roughly 82% in 5-4 splits but was far lower in unanimous rulings — the genuinely contested cases leak the most signal.

flashcards.prompt: Why is a prediction model that gets ~66% of case winners right not necessarily impressive here?

choices.text: Because always betting on the petitioner already wins about 68% of the time
Because the Supreme Court decides too few cases to measure
Because oral argument transcripts are not public

flashcards.explanation_html: A model has to beat the simple baseline to be adding information. The petitioner usually wins, so that alone sets a high bar to clear.

flashcards.prompt: Besides skepticism, what else can heavy questioning of an advocate reflect?
flashcards.back_html: The sheer importance or difficulty of the case. Justices sometimes probe hardest on the side they intend to favor, which is where the question-counting rule breaks down.
